title: Deterministic methods for mixed integer nonlinear programming
contribution: Rebuilds outer approximation for convex MINLPs with integer variables entering nonlinearly. A corrected master program handles infeasible subproblems, and a simpler finiteness proof is given. Quadratic OA, QP/NLP-based B&B and an OA-style Lagrangean decomposition are added, OA is extended to nonsmooth and to nonconvex/inexact settings through a tolerance framework, and a five-code comparison yields a class-based rule of thumb.
problem_entry: Tests Duran-Grossmann OA: its superiority rests on problems linear in y, and its master is not equivalent to P. Restates P with nonlinear y under assumptions A1-A4, said to be weaker than D-G's, and says where each is relaxed (pp. 11, 14-15, 46, 63); also checks Gupta-Ravindran's linear-time claim against his own runs (p. 9).
key_idea: Master program from projection plus linearizations at NLP solutions, with infeasible y cut by linearizations at the phase I solution (pp. 47-53). Curvature enters the master objective only (quadratic OA, QP/NLP-BB), so finiteness is kept (pp. 64-70). MIQP child bounds come from one dual active-set step on the parent tableau (pp. 38-41).
assumptions: A1 convex f, g with X a compact polyhedron; A2 C1; A3 CQ at every NLP(y) solution, shown essential by a cycling example; A4 exact NLP solves; |Y| finite (pp. 15, 61-62). Ch. 8 replaces A1 by A1' (convex g plus linear underestimators of f) and A4 by tolerances eps1-eps3 (pp. 95-96).
proof_devices: Finiteness by non-repetition: strict UBD bound plus no linearized feasible descent direction under the CQ (Theorem 5.2.1, pp. 61-62)
Multiplier aggregation with KKT of the weighted phase I problem F excludes infeasible y and shows only strongly active constraints are needed (Lemma 4.2.1, p. 51)
OA cuts aggregated with lambda plus KKT give exactly the Benders cut, so OA dominates (pp. 56-57, 90)
Bolzano-Weierstrass subsequence plus Cauchy-Schwarz for bounded infinite Y (Theorem 5.5.1, pp. 75-76)
Subdifferential outer approximation with monotone h; penalty-parameter bounds A5 for exact-penalty equivalence (Theorems 7.2.1-7.2.2, pp. 85-87)

Tolerance chain eps0 > eps1+eps2+eps3, with eps0 non-decreasing, gives eps0-optimal finiteness; lower bounds (8.12) and (8.15) from solver tolerances, multipliers and gradient norms (pp. 97-98, 102-103)
Pardalos-Rosen LP underestimator, with the dual LP showing p+1 active constraints (pp. 99-100)
Flop count of child-bound computation before testing (pp. 41-42)

Small computed counterexamples: D-G master (p. 49), CQ cycling (p. 62), linear-OA worst case (pp. 63-64, 69), quadratic-OA worst case exp(-y) (p. 66), -ln(x+1) (p. 66), Viswanathan-Grossmann stopping rule (p. 95), Kocis-Grossmann tests (pp. 93-94)
experiments: MIQP B&B with three branching rules on Beale/HS76/AVGAS/AFIRO/QAP/random problems, counting QPs generated and solved and CPU, failures kept (pp. 43-45). Five MINLP codes on 22 problems: same NLP-relaxation start and same eps-termination; CPU, LP/QP and NLP counts, with the LP/QP count preferred; missing quadratic-OA runs explained; own B&B compared with D-G counts; BATCH vs BATCH-int formulations; three-row Rule of Thumb (pp. 77-83). No experiments for Chs. 7-8.
positioning: Continues and corrects Duran-Grossmann, Yuan et al. and Quesada-Grossmann, naming the faulty step (pp. 46, 49, 67); follows Geoffrion and Flippo et al. on Benders (pp. 10, 53-57); criticises Lazimy, Amir-Hasegawa, Davydov-Sigal, Li, Kocis-Grossmann and Viswanathan-Grossmann by the guarantees they give up (pp. 10-14, 27, 93-95); builds on Fletcher's book and bqpd (pp. 22-23, 31, 77).
writing: Chapter openings state improvements over named work; every algorithm is followed by a computed small example with a figure; first-person judgements kept apart from theorems ('It seems to me' p. 13, 'I do not regard' p. 75, 'in my view' p. 105); results condensed to a Rule of Thumb table (p. 83); minor inconsistency, two classes (p. 79) vs three classes (p. 105).
limits_future: Convexity is the main restriction (p. 15); MIQP software scarce (p. 66); bqpd round-off (p. 79); NAG gives no phase I solution (p. 80); home-made MILP solver may handicap OA (p. 80); nonconvex method rigorous only for concave pure-integer objectives (pp. 99-100). Future: adaptive eps0 reported with the solution (p. 103); global algorithms for nonconvex classes via the framework (p. 105).

method_links.note: At least seven hand-computed smallest counterexamples; hypothesis check (OA evidence limited to problems linear in y) before the remedy; his own quadratic OA given its own worst case
Same start and same eps for all codes; meters with weaknesses; the counter immune to differing QP solvers preferred; failures kept; rule of thumb by class; own handicaps stated

Quadratic-OA runs on BATCH and GTD dropped from the tables (reason given: bqpd round-off, would distort results); the thesis rule of thumb has a third row (QP/NLP-BB for large-gap general-integer problems) that the skill omits

Pre-history: packaged NAG solver limits (one warm-start level, no phase I output, so an extra feasibility NLP) named as a cost; where he owns the code (MILP/MIQP B&B on bqpd) he uses hot starts and pricing from the final tableau
NLP toolkit (SQP, exact penalties, subdifferentials, active-set QP) carried into MINLP; quadratic OA read as SQP for integers
Appendix A gives each test problem with its NLP-relaxation value and integer optimum; NLP/LP test problems converted to MINLP/MIQP; formulation variants kept (BATCH and BATCH-int)

The smaller nonconvex BATCH-int beats the convexified binary BATCH (about 20% of the time), which qualifies the linear>convex>nonconvex ordering; warns that reformulation hides nonlinearity; rejects penalty reformulations that make a convex MINLP a nonconvex NLP

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Infeasibility handling proved against a generic weighted phase I problem F that covers l1, l-infinity and sequential phase I approaches, so the master is correct for any NLP code
Outer termination tolerance eps0 > eps1+eps2+eps3, with lower bounds computed from NLP/MILP tolerances, multipliers and gradient norms and reported with the solution

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: paired worst cases mark out the class
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Worst case for linear OA solved by quadratic OA, then the worst case for quadratic OA solved by linear OA; the pair becomes the binary vs general-integer rule of thumb

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: reinterpret one method as another to compare cuts
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Benders cut = OA cuts aggregated with lambda; quadratic OA = SQP for integers; B&B = clever rounding

transferable: Test an equivalence claim on the smallest instance before building on it (one continuous variable, y in {-1,1}) (p. 49)
Write theory against an abstract class of solver outputs (phase I weights w and feasibility problem F) so that it holds for any NLP code (pp. 49-51)
For every remedy, construct its own worst case, and turn the pair into a class-based recommendation (pp. 63-66, 83)
Prove dominance of one cut family by aggregating the stronger cuts with KKT multipliers to recover the weaker (pp. 56-57)
Price child nodes from the parent's final factorization with one dual active-set step; count the flops before experimenting (pp. 38-42)
Make the termination tolerance computed, bounded below by the inner solvers' tolerances times multiplier and gradient norms, and report it with the answer (pp. 96-103)

Solver comparison: same start, same eps-termination, a counter immune to subsolver differences, every missing entry explained, own baseline checked against the competitor's published counts (pp. 78-81)
Publish each test instance with its relaxation value and integer optimum (pp. 106-113)
coauthors: none (sole-author PhD thesis; supervisor not named in the file)

quotes.text: However, for outer approximation the constraint qualification is more important than has previously been recognised.
This observation implies that the difference between a good implementation of the branch–and–bound algorithm and the outer approximation routines is not as big as originally thought.
